questions.stem: The rusting of iron (Fe) in moist air — 4Fe + 3O₂ + 6H₂O → 4Fe(OH)₃ — is an example of:
questions.explanation: RUSTING — corrosion of IRON in MOIST AIR; an ELECTROCHEMICAL process that is a form of OXIDATION (iron loses electrons) and therefore a REDOX reaction. Required: (a) IRON (Fe); (b) OXYGEN (O₂); (c) WATER (H₂O). If either oxygen OR water is absent, iron won't rust — that's why we paint, oil, grease, galvanise (zinc coating), tin-plate, chrome-plate, or alloy iron (stainless steel with Cr) to prevent rust. Saline/acidic conditions ACCELERATE rusting. CHEMISTRY: Fe is oxidised to Fe²⁺, which further oxidises to Fe³⁺; combining with water gives hydrated iron(III) oxide Fe₂O₃·xH₂O — the reddish-brown flaky substance we call RUST. Unlike aluminium's Al₂O₃ oxide layer (which is dense + protective), rust FLAKES off exposing fresh Fe → continues corroding → structural failure over time. CORROSION varieties: (1) DRY oxidation (at high T, direct O-Fe); (2) WET / ELECTROCHEMICAL (normal rusting); (3) GALVANIC (dissimilar metals in contact + electrolyte); (4) PITTING, STRESS, INTERGRANULAR. METALS & THEIR CORROSION: (a) SILVER → tarnishes BLACK (Ag₂S) in sulfur-containing air; (b) COPPER → develops GREEN patina (basic copper carbonate Cu₂(OH)₂CO₃, ‘verdigris’ as on Statue of Liberty); (c) ALUMINIUM → thin tough Al₂O₃ layer (passivation); (d) BRASS → tarnishes greenish; (e) BRONZE → green patina. PREVENTION: GALVANISATION (Zn on Fe — sacrificial anode), TINNING (Sn on Fe — protects by barrier), CHROME-plating, PAINTING, OILING, ENAMELLING, ALLOYING (stainless steel: Fe + Cr 10-12% + Ni). REDOX mnemonic: OIL RIG — Oxidation Is Loss (of e⁻), Reduction Is Gain (of e⁻). In rusting: Fe is oxidised (LOSES electrons); O₂ is reduced (GAINS electrons). iron loses electrons to oxygen; hydrated iron(III) oxide (Fe₂O₃·xH₂O, reddish-brown) is rust.

questions.stem: The reaction ‘Zn + CuSO₄ → ZnSO₄ + Cu’ is an example of:
questions.explanation: DISPLACEMENT REACTION — a single element displaces another from its compound. Driven by the ACTIVITY SERIES of metals. In this case, ZINC (more reactive) displaces COPPER (less reactive) from COPPER SULPHATE: Zn(s) + CuSO₄(aq) → ZnSO₄(aq) + Cu(s). Observations: blue CuSO₄ solution fades (Cu²⁺ ions consumed); reddish-brown Cu deposits on Zn strip; Zn dissolves. ACTIVITY SERIES of metals (most reactive to least): K > Na > Ca > Mg > Al > Zn > Fe > Pb > H > Cu > Hg > Ag > Au > Pt. Any metal higher in the list will DISPLACE any metal below it from its aqueous salt solution. EXAMPLES: (1) Fe + CuSO₄ → FeSO₄ + Cu (used in classroom demos). (2) Cu + FeSO₄ → NO reaction (Cu less reactive than Fe). (3) Mg + HCl → MgCl₂ + H₂↑ (metal displacing hydrogen from acid). (4) Au, Pt do NOT react with most acids — hence ‘noble metals’ (only dissolve in AQUA REGIA = 3:1 conc HCl:HNO₃). 5 MAJOR TYPES OF REACTIONS: (I) COMBINATION (A+B→AB): 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO; (II) DECOMPOSITION (AB→A+B): 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (electrolysis), CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (heating of limestone); (III) DISPLACEMENT (A+BC → AC+B) — single displacement; (IV) DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT / METATHESIS (AB + CD → AD + CB): AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl↓ (white precipitate) + NaNO₃; (V) REDOX — includes combustion, rusting, photosynthesis, cellular respiration. PRECIPITATION reactions are a subset of double-displacement where an insoluble product forms. NEUTRALISATION: acid + base → salt + water, e.g., HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O (exothermic). Zn, being more reactive than Cu, displaces Cu from CuSO₄; single displacement / metal displacement.

questions.stem: The thermal decomposition of calcium carbonate in a limekiln — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ — produces which commercially valuable product?
questions.explanation: LIME KILN REACTION: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g) at ~900-1000°C; example of THERMAL DECOMPOSITION. PRODUCTS: (1) CaO = CALCIUM OXIDE = ‘QUICKLIME’ / ‘BURNT LIME’ — highly exothermic reaction with water: CaO + H₂O → Ca(OH)₂ (SLAKED LIME, ‘white-wash’) + heat. Used in cement (~60% of a bag), steel-making (flux), purification of sugar, leather tanning, water softening, desulphurisation of flue gas (flue gas + lime → gypsum), glass manufacturing. (2) CO₂ — greenhouse gas released; cement industry is ~8% of global CO₂ emissions (split between limestone decomp + fuel burning). Indian cement industry major CO₂ source. CHEMICAL ‘NICKNAMES’ (VERY common exam topic): Chemical → common name: (a) CaCO₃ = LIMESTONE / CALCITE / MARBLE / CHALK (all CaCO₃ in different crystal forms); (b) CaO = QUICKLIME; (c) Ca(OH)₂ = SLAKED LIME / MILK OF LIME; (d) CaSO₄·½H₂O = PLASTER OF PARIS (gypsum heated to 150°C drives off water: 2CaSO₄·2H₂O → 2CaSO₄·½H₂O + 3H₂O); (e) CaSO₄·2H₂O = GYPSUM; (f) CaOCl₂ = BLEACHING POWDER (chloride of lime); (g) NaHCO₃ = BAKING SODA; (h) Na₂CO₃·10H₂O = WASHING SODA (from solvay process); (i) NaOH = CAUSTIC SODA; (j) H₂SO₄ = OIL OF VITRIOL, ‘KING of CHEMICALS’; (k) HNO₃ = AQUA FORTIS; (l) HCl = MURIATIC ACID; (m) FeSO₄·7H₂O = GREEN VITRIOL; (n) CuSO₄·5H₂O = BLUE VITRIOL; (o) ZnSO₄·7H₂O = WHITE VITRIOL; (p) AgNO₃ = LUNAR CAUSTIC; (q) NH₄Cl = SAL AMMONIAC; (r) KNO₃ = NITER / INDIAN SALTPETRE; (s) NaNO₃ = CHILE SALTPETRE; (t) Mg(OH)₂ = MILK OF MAGNESIA. USES of PoP: casts for broken bones, moulds, statues, wall ceilings — rapid setting with water. used in cement, steel making, flue-gas desulphurisation, paper, water treatment; calcium oxide, CaO.

questions.explanation: EXOTHERMIC vs ENDOTHERMIC — classification of reactions by HEAT flow: (1) EXOTHERMIC — reaction RELEASES heat to surroundings; products have LOWER enthalpy than reactants, so ΔH (enthalpy change) is NEGATIVE. Examples: (a) COMBUSTION — burning of wood, LPG, candle; CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O + heat; (b) RUSTING (slow exothermic, heat barely noticed); (c) NEUTRALISATION — HCl + NaOH → NaCl + H₂O + heat (test-tube warms); (d) CELLULAR RESPIRATION — C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + energy (ATP); (e) SETTING of CEMENT / PLASTER OF PARIS; (f) DISSOLVING of NaOH or H₂SO₄ in water; (g) FORMATION of most IONIC compounds; (h) CONDENSATION of steam → water. (2) ENDOTHERMIC — reaction ABSORBS heat; ΔH > 0. Examples: (a) PHOTOSYNTHESIS — 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + hν → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ (uses sunlight energy); (b) THERMAL DECOMPOSITION — CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂ (needs 900°C heat input); (c) ELECTROLYSIS of water — 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂ (needs electric energy); (d) DISSOLVING of AMMONIUM NITRATE in water (used in cold packs — container gets cold); (e) MELTING of ice (absorbs 334 kJ/kg latent heat); (f) BOILING of water (2260 kJ/kg). The LAW of CONSERVATION of ENERGY: heat released by exothermic reaction = reduction in chemical bond energy (bonds formed stronger than bonds broken). First law of THERMODYNAMICS: ΔU = q + w (internal energy change = heat added + work done on system). Hess's law: net enthalpy change is independent of path. IMPORTANT EXAM fact: when sulphuric acid is diluted, always add ACID to WATER (not water to acid) — the reaction is HIGHLY exothermic, and if water is added to concentrated H₂SO₄, water boils on contact, spattering acid.

questions.stem: The HABER-BOSCH process is used industrially to produce:
questions.explanation: HABER-BOSCH PROCESS — industrial synthesis of AMMONIA (NH₃) from atmospheric NITROGEN (N₂) and HYDROGEN (H₂). Reaction: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) ⇌ 2NH₃(g) + heat (exothermic, ΔH = -92 kJ/mol, reversible). CONDITIONS: (a) high PRESSURE — 150-250 atm (forward rxn reduces moles, so high P favours product per Le Chatelier); (b) moderate-high TEMPERATURE — 400-500°C (high T favours reverse rxn but needed for kinetics — compromise T); (c) IRON (Fe) CATALYST with molybdenum/aluminium oxide promoters (Mittasch 1910); (d) yield per pass only ~15-20% — unreacted N₂ + H₂ recycled in loop. HISTORY: (1) FRITZ HABER (German chemist) developed the process in a lab 1908-09; WON NOBEL in CHEMISTRY 1918 (controversially — he also developed chemical weapons used in WWI — Zyklon A/B, chlorine gas; considered ‘father of chemical warfare’). (2) CARL BOSCH (BASF chemist/engineer) scaled it up industrially by 1913; WON NOBEL 1931 for high-pressure chemistry. TOGETHER: ‘Haber-Bosch Process’ — named Chemistry Landmark. IMPACT: dubbed one of the most IMPORTANT inventions of the 20th century. Before 1910, nitrogen fertilisers came from CHILEAN SALTPETRE (NaNO₃ deposits) and guano (bird droppings, Peru) — both finite. Haber-Bosch made NITROGEN fertiliser MANUFACTURE limitless. Currently: produces ~175 MT of ammonia annually → ~80% used for fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate, DAP, NPK) → feeds nearly HALF the world population. WITHOUT Haber-Bosch, world agriculture could not support >3-4 billion. ENVIRONMENTAL COST: process uses 1-2% of GLOBAL ENERGY; emits ~1-2% of global CO₂; runaway N-fertiliser use has caused massive eutrophication (algal blooms), groundwater nitrate pollution, GHG emissions (N₂O). INDIA: world's 2nd-largest urea producer and consumer; relies on imported natural gas (H₂ feedstock) + imported/subsidised urea. Recent push: NEEM-COATED UREA, NANO UREA (IFFCO, 2021 — nano nitrogen, 500 ml bottle replaces 45 kg bag), green ammonia (from green H₂, a key NGHM 2023 outcome). from N₂ + H₂ under high T (~450°C) + high P (~200 atm) + Fe catalyst; basis of nitrogenous fertilisers (urea, ammonium nitrate) that feed ~half the world.

questions.explanation: CATALYST — substance that INCREASES the RATE of a chemical reaction without being consumed or permanently altered by it. Works by providing an ALTERNATIVE REACTION PATHWAY with LOWER ACTIVATION ENERGY (Ea). Since it affects FORWARD and REVERSE rates EQUALLY, it does NOT change the EQUILIBRIUM POSITION or ΔH (enthalpy change) — only helps equilibrium get there FASTER. TYPES of catalysts: (1) POSITIVE — increases rate (most common; ‘catalyst’ usually means this). (2) NEGATIVE / INHIBITOR — decreases rate. (3) AUTOCATALYST — a PRODUCT of the reaction that catalyses further reaction. (4) HOMOGENEOUS — same phase as reactants (e.g., conc. H₂SO₄ in esterification). (5) HETEROGENEOUS — different phase (e.g., solid Fe catalysing gaseous Haber-Bosch). (6) BIOCATALYSTS / ENZYMES — biological proteins (amylase, pepsin, lipase — act at mild body temp, highly specific). FAMOUS INDUSTRIAL CATALYSTS + processes: (a) HABER-BOSCH — Fe (Mo-promoted) for NH₃; (b) CONTACT PROCESS — V₂O₅ (vanadium pentoxide) for H₂SO₄ via 2SO₂ + O₂ → 2SO₃; (c) OSTWALD PROCESS — Pt/Rh gauze for HNO₃ via 4NH₃ + 5O₂ → 4NO + 6H₂O; (d) HYDROGENATION of vegetable oils — Ni (Ni-catalysed hydrogenation of unsaturated oils to solid ‘vanaspati’ / margarine); (e) CATALYTIC CRACKING (petroleum) — zeolites, alumina; (f) CATALYTIC CONVERTERS in vehicles — Pt/Pd/Rh — convert CO → CO₂, NOx → N₂ + O₂, unburnt HC → CO₂ + H₂O; (g) ZIEGLER-NATTA catalysts — for polymerisation of alkenes (Ziegler + Natta, Nobel 1963, TiCl₄ + AlEt₃). CATALYST POISONING — certain impurities block active sites (e.g., Pb in petrol poisons catalytic converters — hence unleaded petrol is mandatory). ENZYMES: (a) AMYLASE — starch to maltose (saliva); (b) PEPSIN — protein in acidic stomach; (c) TRYPSIN — pancreas; (d) LIPASE — fats; (e) DNA POLYMERASE — DNA replication; (f) RNA POLYMERASE — transcription; (g) RIBOZYMES — RNA catalysts. Enzymes are extremely specific (lock-key / induced-fit); rate enhancement can be 10⁶-10²⁰ times. speeds up the forward AND reverse reaction equally; does not alter equilibrium position or ΔH; is itself NOT consumed.

questions.stem: BAKING SODA is sodium bicarbonate (NaHCO₃). When it's HEATED, it decomposes according to: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. The CO₂ released causes:

options.option_text: The BAKED ITEM (cake, bread) to RISE / become POROUS

questions.explanation: BAKING SODA (NaHCO₃, sodium bicarbonate/sodium hydrogen carbonate) — decomposes on heating: 2NaHCO₃ → Na₂CO₃ + H₂O + CO₂. The released CO₂ gas creates BUBBLES in the batter/dough that EXPAND during baking, making the cake/bread RISE and become FLUFFY / POROUS. DOWNSIDE: pure baking soda leaves behind sodium carbonate (Na₂CO₃) which has a BITTER / soapy taste → that’s why bakers use BAKING POWDER instead. BAKING POWDER = NaHCO₃ + a mild EDIBLE ACID (e.g., TARTARIC ACID / cream of tartar, or MONOCALCIUM PHOSPHATE) + cornstarch (anti-caking). When water/moisture added + heat, NaHCO₃ + tartaric acid → sodium tartrate (tasteless) + H₂O + CO₂. The tartaric acid neutralises the bitter Na₂CO₃, giving a CLEAN taste. DOUBLE-ACTING BAKING POWDER: contains two acids — one fast-acting (reacts on mixing with water), one slow-acting (only on heating). Yeast is another leavening agent (living yeast fermentation: C₆H₁₂O₆ → 2 C₂H₅OH + 2 CO₂ + energy) — used in bread, pizza, beer. Uses of BAKING SODA beyond baking: (1) FIRE EXTINGUISHERS — CO₂ smothers fire; (2) MEDICINE — antacid (neutralises HCl in stomach: NaHCO₃ + HCl → NaCl + H₂O + CO₂); (3) CLEANING — mild abrasive; (4) PERSONAL CARE — deodorant, toothpaste; (5) SODA-ACID fire extinguisher (old type) — NaHCO₃ sol + H₂SO₄ → CO₂ foam; (6) BUFFER in biological systems (blood pH regulation via HCO₃⁻/H₂CO₃). WASHING SODA (Na₂CO₃·10H₂O) uses: (1) removing permanent hardness of water (precipitates Ca²⁺, Mg²⁺); (2) glass, soap, paper manufacture; (3) cleaning. trapped CO₂ bubbles expand during baking.

questions.stem: AQUA REGIA (‘royal water’), which can dissolve even gold and platinum, is a mixture of:

options.option_text: 3 parts CONC. HCl + 1 part CONC. HNO₃ (by volume)

questions.explanation: AQUA REGIA (Latin: ‘royal water’ / ‘king's water’) — a mixture of 3 parts concentrated HYDROCHLORIC ACID (HCl) + 1 part concentrated NITRIC ACID (HNO₃) by volume. Known since medieval alchemy (~8th-century Islamic alchemist Jabir ibn Hayyan / Geber) as it could dissolve GOLD and PLATINUM — the ‘royal metals’ — which neither acid alone can dissolve. REACTION: HNO₃ (oxidising agent) oxidises Cl⁻ from HCl to give NASCENT CHLORINE (Cl) + NITROSYL CHLORIDE (NOCl), both of which are highly reactive species; gold is first oxidised to Au³⁺ by nitric acid, and then chloride ions form stable [AuCl₄]⁻ (tetrachloroaurate) complex, removing Au³⁺ from equilibrium and driving the reaction forward. Au + HNO₃ + 4HCl → H[AuCl₄] + NO + 2H₂O. Similarly Pt → [PtCl₆]²⁻. USES: dissolving GOLD in refining and electrochemistry; etching / cleaning of precious metal residues; historically, used to ESCAPE NAZI theft — Hungarian chemist GEORGE DE HEVESY dissolved Nobel gold medals of JAMES FRANCK + MAX VON LAUE in aqua regia, stored the solution in Copenhagen, recovered gold after WWII. NEITHER HCl nor HNO₃ alone dissolves gold. TITANIUM, IRIDIUM, RUTHENIUM, OSMIUM, RHODIUM do NOT dissolve in aqua regia either (truly ‘noble’ in that sense). OTHER ACID FACTS: (1) HF (hydrofluoric acid) is used to etch GLASS (SiO₂ + 4HF → SiF₄↑ + 2H₂O); stored in wax/plastic, not glass. (2) CONCENTRATED sulphuric acid is HIGHLY HYGROSCOPIC and DEHYDRATING — will char sugar/cotton/wood to black carbon. (3) PHOSPHORIC ACID (H₃PO₄) — in cola drinks (flavouring + preservative); fertiliser manufacture. (4) CITRIC ACID — in citrus fruits, lemon. (5) LACTIC ACID — curd/sour milk, sore muscles. (6) OXALIC ACID — spinach, rhubarb (can cause kidney stones in excess). (7) FORMIC ACID — ant stings, nettles. formed ~1:3 mix of nitric:hydrochloric; nascent Cl₂ + NOCl species attack noble metals.

questions.stem: PHOTOSYNTHESIS (6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂) is an example of:
questions.explanation: PHOTOSYNTHESIS — the biological process by which GREEN PLANTS, algae, and cyanobacteria convert LIGHT energy into CHEMICAL energy, storing it in the bonds of glucose (and ultimately all carbohydrates, amino acids, lipids). The reaction: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + light energy → C₆H₁₂O₆ (glucose) + 6O₂. TAKES PLACE in: CHLOROPLASTS (in plant/algae cells) — contain CHLOROPHYLL (green pigment) which absorbs mainly RED + BLUE light (reflects green, hence plants look green). TWO STAGES: (1) LIGHT-DEPENDENT (or ‘photo’) reactions — in THYLAKOID membranes; photons split WATER (photolysis: 2H₂O → 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ + O₂), generating O₂ (released as waste), ATP, NADPH. (2) LIGHT-INDEPENDENT / CALVIN CYCLE (‘dark’ reactions, misnomer — still need products of light phase) — in STROMA; CO₂ is FIXED onto ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate (RuBP) by enzyme RuBisCO (most abundant protein on Earth); then reduced using ATP+NADPH to glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate (G3P) → glucose. CLASSIFICATION: (1) ENDOTHERMIC — absorbs energy (solar → chemical); ΔH > 0. (2) REDOX — CO₂ is REDUCED (gains electrons, to form C-H bonds of glucose); H₂O is OXIDISED (loses electrons, releases O₂). (3) PHOTOCHEMICAL — requires LIGHT. (4) COMBINATION + REARRANGEMENT on atomic scale. IMPORTANCE: (1) produces ~100% of atmospheric O₂ (with plants + marine phytoplankton both major); (2) foundation of ALL food chains (autotrophy); (3) removes ~100 GtC/year of CO₂ from atmosphere; (4) source of fossil fuels (ancient photosynthesis). C3, C4, CAM plants — different variants of carbon fixation; C4 (maize, sugarcane) more efficient at high temperatures; CAM (cactus, pineapple) fix CO₂ at night to reduce water loss. OPPOSITE of photosynthesis: CELLULAR RESPIRATION (in mitochondria) — C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O + ATP energy; exothermic redox; opposite arrow. Together: the CARBON CYCLE on biological scale. Chlorophyll-a (the main pigment, blue-green, absorbs ~430+660 nm), Chl-b (accessory, yellow-green); also carotenoids (β-carotene, xanthophylls — yellows/oranges seen in autumn leaves when chl breaks down). uses light energy; CO₂ is reduced (gains H to form glucose), water is oxidised (loses H, releases O₂); chlorophyll absorbs photons.

questions.stem: Mixing AgNO₃ (silver nitrate) with NaCl (sodium chloride) solution produces a WHITE PRECIPITATE of:

options.option_text: AgCl (SILVER CHLORIDE) — a DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT + PRECIPITATION reaction; AgCl is insoluble in water, white, turns grey in light (photosensitive) — basis of traditional photography

questions.explanation: AgNO₃(aq) + NaCl(aq) → AgCl(s)↓ + NaNO₃(aq) — a DOUBLE DISPLACEMENT (metathesis) reaction that is ALSO a PRECIPITATION reaction. Drive: AgCl has VERY LOW solubility in water (Ksp ~ 1.8 × 10⁻¹⁰), so it precipitates out as a WHITE curdy solid. In light, AgCl darkens to Ag (metallic) + Cl₂ — this PHOTOCHEMICAL reaction was the basis of traditional black-and-white PHOTOGRAPHY (silver halide photographic film). 2AgCl → 2Ag + Cl₂ (in sunlight). Test in chemistry lab: adding dilute AgNO₃ to an unknown solution and getting a white curdy precipitate that dissolves in excess NH₃ → confirms Cl⁻ ion. Similarly: with Br⁻ → PALE YELLOW AgBr (slight solubility in dilute NH₃); with I⁻ → YELLOW AgI (insoluble even in concentrated NH₃). This is the systematic test for halide ions. OTHER FAMOUS PRECIPITATION TESTS: (1) Pb(NO₃)₂ + 2KI → PbI₂ (BRIGHT YELLOW) + 2KNO₃ — ‘GOLDEN RAIN’ experiment. (2) BaCl₂ + Na₂SO₄ → BaSO₄ (WHITE) + 2NaCl — barium sulphate precipitation test for SO₄²⁻ ion; also barium meal for X-rays. (3) CaCl₂ + Na₂CO₃ → CaCO₃ (WHITE) + 2NaCl — hard water softening. (4) CuSO₄ + NaOH → Cu(OH)₂ (LIGHT BLUE) + Na₂SO₄. (5) FeCl₃ + 3NaOH → Fe(OH)₃ (RUSTY BROWN) + 3NaCl — iron identification. (6) AgNO₃ + NH₄OH → grey/black Ag₂O precipitate initially, dissolves in excess NH₃ to form diamminesilver(I) [Ag(NH₃)₂]⁺ — basis of TOLLEN’s REAGENT (silver mirror test for aldehydes). (7) Mg²⁺ + OH⁻ → Mg(OH)₂ (WHITE GELATINOUS) — ‘milk of magnesia’ nearly insoluble. (8) NH₄Cl + AgNO₃ → AgCl (WHITE) + NH₄NO₃. Precipitation is a way to test for ions, and industrially to PURIFY (drop out) unwanted species, or to manufacture pigments.
